BoardRegion.description:
Which regional deployment of a multi-region ATS holds a tenant's board.

Lever runs separate data-residency deployments — `api.lever.co` and
`api.eu.lever.co` — with **separate tenant namespaces**. A global tenant
asked for on the EU host answers 404 `{"ok":false,"error":"Document not
found"}`, byte-identical to what either host answers for a site name that
does not exist anywhere.

That identical 404 is why the region has to be carried rather than assumed.
A wrong region is indistinguishable from a wrong board token, so an EU
tenant fetched from the global host does not fail with a message naming the
problem: the listing is invalidated, `scanned` is 0, and every run reads
`failed` with no hint of the cause. Recognising an EU URL while fetching the
global host would manufacture exactly that.

`None` on a company means "this family has one deployment" (Greenhouse,
Ashby, Google), which is why the stored column is nullable rather than
defaulting to `GLOBAL` — absent and global-by-choice are different records.
BoardRegion.title: BoardRegion

ScopeCells.description:
The joint over role x band x track x locations x domains.

Every other count in this response is a MARGINAL — per band, per domain,
per location — and marginals cannot be intersected. `domain_counts` in
particular counts a multi-label posting once per domain, so they do not
even sum. This is the one shape a client can apply the real gate to.

Interned: `cells` is a list of six integers, `[role, band, track,
location_set, domain_set, count]`, indexing the five dictionaries beside
it. The dictionaries are the only place a slug is spelled out, which is
what keeps a large catalog small.

`location_sets[i]` is never empty — a posting with no matched location
never reaches the catalog. `domain_sets[i]` IS empty for an unclassified
posting, which passes the domain axis whatever the user selected; a client
that drops the empty set re-implements the gate wrongly.

Three states, kept apart because they have different cures. `companies`
are counted. `missing_companies` are TRACKED but not catalogued — nothing
is known about them yet, and onboarding one must not blank the screen,
which is why `ready` does not consult them (`joint_counts_ready` does).
`stale_companies` hold postings this column cannot place, from a scan that
predates it; their next COMPLETE scan clears them. `ready` is false while
any remain, because a partial joint is a WRONG number rather than a small
one — but they are named, so the wait is diagnosable instead of a boolean.
ScopeCells.title: ScopeCells

get.description:
Search every other company RoleBand can scan, by name.

Server-side because the set is thousands of companies: the register

put.description:
Follow every other company RoleBand can scan, or stop.

Following starts the background scan (`workflows.directory_sweep`), which
follows each company it finds roles at. Stopping switches off exactly the
companies the set brought in and remembers them, so following again brings
back the same ones; a company followed by name is never touched.

get.description:
The whole set as the register draws it: its size, whether it is followed,
and how far the background scan has read it. A pure read.

Job-seeker sectors merged with the user's current tracking state.

The Company Explorer's first paint depends on this and nothing else, so it
is a pure read: no `ensure_builtins()` upsert+commit (startup, the pipeline,
and every mutating company route already reconcile built-ins — a GET that
writes can queue behind a running scrape's row locks and hold the whole
screen blank), and no `jobs` aggregate. Open-role counts arrive separately
via `/api/companies/open-counts`.

Each company's name by slug: every catalog company, and every tracked
one, whose stored name wins. The dashboard reads it once, before its first
render, so every screen names a company the way the company does ("PwC",
"CrowdStrike") rather than by its slug, including the level table's
reference companies on an install that follows none of them. The
directory's thousands of other companies are not in it.

Open in-scope role count per company slug.

Split out of `/api/companies/discovery` so the roster renders immediately
and each row fills its count in place. Companies with no open in-scope role
are absent; the caller reads a missing slug as 0.

Beside it, per followed company, what the Profile's count leaves out and
how many of its roles no answer can keep, by reason, so each status
shows where the company is.

put.description:
Atomically follow and unfollow the companies the person switched.

A company the change does not name keeps its state. Missing discovery
companies are registered first. Sources without an implemented adapter
remain ``pending`` and therefore cannot be scraped yet; the selection
records intent without overstating connector readiness. Unfollowed rows are
paused rather than deleted, preserving their history.

Shadow the complete listing, then save the comparison for review.

patch.description:
Toggle a company's tracking (`enabled`) and/or visibility (`visible`).

Both fields are optional and applied independently. Built-in and user-added

post.description:
Start/stop the oMLX managed server, then re-probe and report the truth.

A CLI that exited 0 is not evidence the server answers, so the response
carries the fresh probe rather than the command's own optimism.

Finish an interrupted switch now, without touching the choice.

Its own endpoint rather than a re-PUT of the current tier, because that
would be a different act with two wrong side effects: it records the tier
as a USER choice (the screen would start offering "Choose automatically" to
someone who never chose), and it starts nothing at all — the tier is not
moving, so the switch endpoint correctly treats it as a no-op. The work
owed here is not a choice, it is the remainder of one already made.

Stop the running switch AND put the choice back. One operation.

There is deliberately no endpoint that only kills the job. The corpus is
converted in place, so a bare stop would leave the tier pointing at the
model the user just cancelled with most rows still on the old one — and the
next scheduled pass would finish the switch they believed they had stopped.
The only honest cancel is stop-and-revert.

Order matters. The re-embed is stopped FIRST so no batch can land after the
choice moves back; then the choice is restored in one transaction. A final
batch that slips through during teardown is harmless either way, because
every row carries the tier that produced it — the worst case is a handful of
rows the next pass converts back, not a corpus split across two spaces.

put.description:
Choose which artifact of the bundled model this Mac runs, or restore auto.

Its own endpoint, and a write that costs something: switching re-embeds the
entire corpus, because fp32 and int8 are the same model in *nearly* the
same space, and a corpus half in each ranks against a seam.
So the switch is one transaction plus one detached job, in this order:
record the choice (shared, so every checkout follows), push it to this
checkout's decision file, drop the loaded encoder, then spawn the re-embed.

A no-op switch does none of that. Re-selecting the active tier must not
cost a full re-embed for zero change.

get.description:
Cross-company skill similarity over currently-open roles.

A company's skill set = skill concepts required in at least `min_jobs` of its
open roles (the floor trims one-off mentions that inflate spurious overlap;
industries and competencies are excluded: a vertical is not a skill, and what
every role is expected to do is overlap every company shares). Each pair
is scored by the cosine of rarity-weighted skill vectors (`compute_overlap`).
The companies are those named in `company`, else the top `limit_companies` by
open roles in the scope, shown in an order that puts similar ones together.

The Skills tab: a slice's skills by how characteristic they are
of it, against the whole market; the whole market by share; competencies
apart, industries excluded.

Skill demand over time from the `skill_demand_daily` V2 rollup.

Returns a shared, sorted `dates` axis and one aligned `series` per skill (0-filled
on days with no slice), so the client can draw sparklines without post-processing.
When `term` (concept slug) is omitted the top `limit` skills by their most-recent
count are chosen; otherwise exactly the requested slugs are returned. `days<=0`
means all history. Series exclude industries (they never enter the rollup).

History accrues one slice-set per pipeline run from the first run that extracted
skills, so a young install's series are near-flat; the client shows an accruing note.

Equity decomposition of open-role comp for the "Stock trajectory" view.

Splits each open role's estimated total comp into base/bonus/equity (see
`comp_split`) and partitions companies into public (equity tracks a listed
ticker, so it flexes with the stock price) vs private/illiquid. The UI applies
a stock-price scenario to the equity slice client-side. The roles
`/api/statistics/compensation` describes: a place set once.

Compensation percentiles over time from the `comp_snapshot` raw daily values.

`dim` selects the grouping (`overall`/`company`/`level`/`family`); returns a
shared sorted `dates` axis + one aligned `series` per key with `{date, p25, p50,
p75, p90}` points (null-filled on days with no slice). `days<=0` = all history.

Percentiles are recomputed here from the raw values of the *visible* companies,
so hiding a company retroactively and exactly removes it from every point in the
series (impossible from `comp_metrics`, whose stored percentiles can't be
re-aggregated). History accrues one snapshot-set per pipeline run.

Compensation across the roles open now: the roles Insights describes.

Two different quantities live in this payload and must not be conflated:

* `overall` / `histogram` / `by_level` / `by_company` / `by_family` / `by_skill`
  aggregate `Job.comp_median`, which is an *imputed total-comp estimate* — a
  lookup keyed by (company, level, family), not anything an employer said. It
  carries very few distinct values, so it is a reference point, not a sample.
* `disclosed` carries the bands employers actually printed in the posting, as
  *base salary* (see `build_disclosed_bands`). Base pay and total comp cannot
  share an axis, so the UI keeps them in separate panels.
* `disclosure` is the *rate* — how many open roles state pay at all, overall
  and per company/level. Basis-independent, and denominated in roles the
  disclosure pass has actually read (see `build_disclosure_rates`).

Coverage is reported so the UI can state how much of the open set is estimated.

No window. Keeping roles FIRST SEEN in the last N days would change the
population, not the period: most open postings are first seen recently, so
a 30-day window is nearly all-time and a 7-day one a sample of whatever was
onboarded that week. The trend routes carry time.

Pay transparency over time from the `disclosure_snapshot` daily cells.

`dim` selects the grouping (`overall`/`company`/`level`); returns a shared
sorted `dates` axis + one aligned `series` per key. Each point carries both
quantities the snapshot separates:

* `rate` = `disclosed / checked` — the share of read open roles stating a pay
  band. Basis-independent; `open - checked` is reported so the UI can show the
  extraction backlog instead of counting it as employer silence.
* `low_p50` / `high_p50` — the median published band, pooled strictly within
  `basis` (base salary). One vote per distinct band, since an employer hangs
  many reqs off one band.

Counts are re-summed here from the raw cells rather than read as stored
aggregates, so hiding a company retroactively and exactly removes it from
every point in the series — the same property `comp-trends` relies on.

Diagnostic: the modeled equity slice checked against employer-stated cash.

For open roles with a stated base band (basis='base'), implied equity =
comp_median − stated base × (1 + bonus share); `build_equity_residuals`
aggregates that per (company, band) and compares it to the modeled equity
share. Deliberately a separate endpoint — this is a model-confidence
surface, not part of the hot compensation payload.

How every company with a reviewed ladder names each level, followed or
not, for the Levels tab. Reference data: it reads no postings, so the
Insights scope and window do not apply. Who is followed comes from
`/api/companies/discovery`, which the screen already reads.

Cockpit aggregate for the Statistics landing tab.

KPI tiles + a short generated brief + highlight strips, pulling from the demand,
skills, and cluster layers. `days<=0` means all-time; otherwise the new/closed
counters are scoped to the last N days of lifecycle events (so the period control
is meaningful as history accrues).

Hiring-velocity motion over a time window (honors the period lens).

Opened / updated / closed activity + net flow from lifecycle events, the aging
distribution of still-open roles, and the observed listing duration of roles
that closed in the window. `days<=0` means all-time. The duration needs a
spread of closed roles, so it accrues with history; the UI flags a thin sample.

It is not a time to fill: it measures how long we observed a posting
advertised, and a public board says nothing about whether anyone was hired.
Freshness + supervision surface for the watchdog and dashboard badge.

post.description:
Queue provider-safe authoritative reconciliation.

Empty selection queues the roster; subset queues those bindings. One
dispatcher pass starts immediately, then the ten-minute agent drains the
remainder. Same-provider bindings never share a shard, and persisted
policy/cooldown gates apply to manual work exactly as scheduled work.

A live run is never joined by a second dispatcher. Companies asked for by
name are queued anyway, and the live run reads them next
(`run_pipeline(join_requests=True)`); asking for everyone queues nothing,
since the live run reads them already. Queue state is committed before
the process starts.

Stop a manual sync and remove its remaining queue priority.

The header control stops only a scan Sync asked for: a scheduled tick or a
first scan is not its to stop. Pending manual bindings have their prior
scheduler deadlines restored; naturally overdue work stays overdue.

It ends only the run it stopped: the live run recorded under the process
group of the scan it asked the supervisor to stop. Dequeuing stops no
process, so on its own it ends no run, and a live run in another group is
not this route's to end.

get.description:
The companies a targeted sync may cover, with what ranking them needs.

The roster is `get_active_targets` and nothing else — exactly the set
`run_pipeline` would accept — so the picker can never offer a company the
run would silently drop. A tracked company with no connector is absent here
on purpose: it is a recorded interest, not a scrapeable source, and the
Companies board is where that distinction is already explained.

A pure read, like `/api/companies/discovery`: no `ensure_builtins()` upsert
(startup and every mutating company route already reconcile built-ins), so
opening the picker can never queue behind a running scrape's row locks.

Per company:
  * `last_sync_at` / `age_hours` / `stale` — the newest reconcile attempted,
    from the runs: "when did we last go and look", not "when did
    we last succeed"; a source we attempted and failed is not fresh, and
    its outcome below is what says so.
  * `last_full_scan_at` — the newest reconcile that read the whole board:
    the coverage clock ("Scanned 3 hours ago").
  * `automatic` — scanned without the user asking (not a user-directed source).
  * `last_outcome` / `retryable` — read off the newest **full** run. A
    targeted run's `per_source` covers only its own subset, so it cannot
    answer "which sources still need work" for anyone else.
